title: Partial Pressures and Mole Fractions
short: Each gas in a mixture pushes as if it were alone: Pᵢ = χᵢ × P(total).
trouble: Students think the gas with heavier molecules supplies more of the pressure, or forget to subtract water's vapor pressure for a gas collected over water.

blocks.html: Air is a mixture: mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon and a little carbon dioxide. How does each gas contribute to the pressure? The The Ideal Gas Law answers that, using the mole fractions you already know.

Dalton's law: in a mixture of gases, each gas exerts the pressure it would have alone in the same container (its partial pressure), and the total is the sum: $$P_\text{total} = P_A + P_B + \cdots, \qquad P_A = \chi_A\,P_\text{total}.$$ A gas collected over water is mixed with water vapor: $P_\text{gas} = P_\text{total} - P_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$.

In an ideal gas the molecules don't interact; each one hits the walls as if the others weren't there. Pressure comes from those hits, and $PV = nRT$ says the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules, $n$, at a given $V$ and $T$, whatever kind they are. So each gas's share of the pressure is its share of the molecules: its mole fraction. A heavy molecule hits harder but moves slower, and at the same temperature the two effects cancel exactly; that is why only the count matters.

opts.task: Add or remove one gas and watch the partial pressures and mole fractions.

blocks.cap: Helium and argon in one box. The partial pressures add to the total, in proportion to the moles of each, not their masses.

blocks.html: Try it in Gas in a Box: mix two gases and read each one's partial pressure.

blocks.title: A mixture of two gases
blocks.q: A tank holds $2.00\ \text{mol}$ of He and $1.00\ \text{mol}$ of Ar at a total pressure of $6.00\ \text{atm}$. Find the partial pressure of each.

blocks.title: Collected over water
blocks.q: Hydrogen gas is collected over water at $25^\circ\text{C}$ in a $0.250\ \text{L}$ tube. The total pressure is $755\ \text{mmHg}$, and water's vapor pressure at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $23.8\ \text{mmHg}$. How many moles of $\mathrm{H_2}$ were collected?

blocks.html: Thinking the gas with heavier molecules supplies more of the pressure, or forgetting the water vapor in a gas collected over water. Pressure depends on the number of molecules, not their mass: in a 1 : 1 mixture of He and Ar, each supplies half. And a tube over water always holds water vapor; subtract its vapor pressure before using $PV = nRT$. Check: the partial pressures must add up to the total.
